title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Granting and Confirmation of Rights
keywords_en: administrative litigation; trial of administrative cases concerning trademark authorization and confirmation
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Circular on Issuing the "Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation"

Fa Fa [2010] No. 12

To the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government, the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army, and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

The Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation of the Supreme People's Court are hereby issued for your diligent implementation.

April 20, 2010

Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation

Since the implementation of the Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China on December 1, 2001, the people's courts have, in accordance with the law, begun to accept and hear administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation filed by interested parties against specific administrative acts of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, such as trademark refusal review, trademark opposition review, trademark dispute, and trademark cancellation review. Active exploration has been made on relevant issues of law application, and relatively rich trial experience has been accumulated. In order to better adjudicate such administrative cases, further summarize trial experience, and clarify and unify trial standards, the Supreme People's Court has convened several special meetings and conducted special research, widely solicited opinions from relevant courts, relevant departments, and experts and scholars, and studied and summarized the issues of law application in the trial of administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation. On this basis, in accordance with the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and other legal provisions, and in light of trial practice, the following opinions are put forward regarding the trial of such cases:

1. When trying administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation, the people's court may, in accordance with the law, appropriately tighten the standards for trademark authorization and confirmation when examining and determining conditions such as trademark similarity and commodity similarity and handling conflicts with prior commercial marks for disputed trademarks that have not yet been put into extensive use, fully consider the interests of consumers and industry peers, effectively curb unfair preemptive registration, focus on protecting the rights and interests of prior commercial marks such as prior trademarks and business names with relatively high reputation and strong distinctiveness, and eliminate the possibility of confusion between commercial marks as much as possible; for disputed trademarks that have been in use for a long time, have established a relatively high market reputation, and have formed a relevant public group, the people's court shall accurately grasp the legislative intent of the Trademark Law to coordinate the protection of prior commercial mark rights and interests with the maintenance of market order, fully respect the market reality that the relevant public has objectively distinguished the relevant commercial marks, and focus on maintaining the market order that has been formed and stabilized.

2. In practice, although some marks or their constituent elements contain exaggerations, they are not sufficient to cause misunderstanding based on daily life experience or the general perception of the relevant public. In such circumstances, the people's court should not readily determine such marks to be marks that are exaggerative and deceptive.

3. When examining and determining whether a relevant mark constitutes a circumstance of having other adverse effects, the people's court shall consider whether the mark or its constituent elements may have negative or adverse effects on the social public interests and public order of China's politics, economy, culture, religion, ethnicity, etc. If the registration of a relevant mark only damages specific civil rights and interests, since the Trademark Law has separately provided for relief methods and corresponding procedures, it is inappropriate to determine that it falls under the circumstance of having other adverse effects.

4. According to the Trademark Law, the names of administrative divisions at or above the county level or foreign geographical names known to the public shall generally not be registered or used as trademarks. In practice, some trademarks are composed of geographical names and other elements. In such circumstances, if the trademark as a whole has distinctive features due to the addition of other elements, and no longer has a geographical meaning or does not take the geographical name as its main meaning, it is inappropriate to determine that the trademark is unregistrable merely because it contains the name of an administrative division at or above the county level or a foreign geographical name known to the public.

5. When trying administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation, the people's court shall examine and determine whether a trademark has distinctive features as a whole based on the general perception of the relevant public of the goods designated for use by the disputed trademark. If the descriptive elements contained in the mark do not affect the mark's overall distinctive features, or if the descriptive mark is presented in a unique manner such that the relevant public can identify the source of goods through it, it shall be determined to have distinctive features.

6. When trying administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation, the people's court shall examine and determine whether a disputed foreign language trademark has distinctive features based on the general perception of the relevant public within China. Even if the foreign language in the disputed mark has an inherent meaning, if the relevant public can identify the source of goods through the mark, it does not affect the determination of its distinctive features.

7. When determining whether a disputed trademark is a generic name, the people's court shall examine whether it belongs to a statutory or customary commodity name. If it belongs to a generic commodity name according to legal provisions or national standards or industry standards, it shall be determined as a generic name. If the relevant public generally believes that a certain name can refer to a category of goods, the name shall be determined as a customary generic name. If a name is listed as a commodity name in professional reference books or dictionaries, it may be used as a reference for determining a customary generic name.

Customary generic names are generally determined based on the general perception of the relevant public nationwide. For goods that are relatively fixed in a relevant market due to historical traditions, local customs, geographical environment, etc., the commonly used appellations within that relevant market may be determined as generic names.

If the applicant knew or should have known that the trademark it applied for registration was a customary commodity name within a certain region, the trademark it applied for registration shall be deemed a generic name.

8. When examining and determining whether a disputed trademark is a generic name, the people's court generally takes the factual status at the time of filing the trademark registration application as the benchmark. If it was not a generic name at the time of application but became a generic name at the time of approval for registration, it shall still be determined as a generic name for the goods; if it was a generic name for the goods at the time of application but was no longer a generic name at the time of approval for registration, it does not prevent it from obtaining registration.

9. If a mark merely or mainly describes or explains the quality, main raw materials, function, use, weight, quantity, place of origin, or other characteristics of the goods on which it is used, it shall be determined to lack distinctive features. If a mark or its constituent elements suggest the characteristics of the goods but do not affect their function of identifying the source of goods, it does not fall under the above circumstances.

10. When trying administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation concerning the protection of well-known trademarks, the people's court may refer to the relevant provisions of Article 5, Article 9, Article 10, etc., of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Involving the Protection of Well-known Trademarks.

11. For well-known trademarks that have been registered in China, when determining the scope of their protection on dissimilar goods, attention shall be paid to the suitability to their degree of well-knownness. For well-known trademarks registered in China that are widely known to the public, when determining the scope of their protection on dissimilar goods, a relatively broad scope of protection suitable to their degree of well-knownness shall be given.

12. If a trademark agent, representative, or agent or representative in the sense of a distribution, agency, or other sales agency relationship, without authorization, registers the trademark of the principal or represented party in its own name, the people's court shall determine that such act constitutes a preemptive registration of the principal's or represented party's trademark by the agent or representative. In trial practice, some preemptive registration acts occur during the stage when the agency or representation relationship is still under negotiation, i.e., the preemptive registration occurs first, and the agency or representation relationship is formed later. In such cases, it shall be regarded as a preemptive registration act by the agent or representative. A trademark registration applicant who colludes with and conspires with the above-mentioned agent or representative to preemptively register may be regarded as an agent or representative. Whether there is collusion and conspiracy to preemptively register may be presumed based on the specific identity relationship between the trademark registration applicant and the above-mentioned agent or representative, among other circumstances.

13. The trademark signs that an agent or representative is not allowed to apply for registration include not only signs identical to the trademark of the principal or represented party but also similar signs; the goods for which an application for registration is not allowed include not only goods identical to those on which the trademark of the principal or represented party is used but also similar goods.

14. When determining commodity similarity and trademark similarity in administrative cases involving trademark authorization and confirmation, the people's court may refer to the relevant provisions of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Trademark Civil Disputes.

15. When examining and determining whether relevant goods or services are similar, the people's court shall consider whether the function, use, production department, sales channels, consumer groups, etc., of the goods are identical or have a relatively strong connection; whether the purpose, content, method, target, etc., of the services are identical or have a relatively strong connection; and whether there is a relatively strong connection between the goods and services, and whether it is easy for the relevant public to believe that the goods or services are provided by the same entity, or that there is a specific connection among their providers. The International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks and the Similar Grouping of Goods and Services may be used as a reference for determining whether goods or services are similar.

16. When determining whether trademarks are similar, the people's court shall consider not only the degree of similarity of the constituent elements of the trademark signs and the overall trademark, but also factors such as the distinctiveness and reputation of the relevant trademarks and the degree of association of the goods on which they are used, with the standard of whether confusion is likely to occur.

17. Article 31 of the Trademark Law, which provides that "the application for trademark registration shall not infringe upon the existing prior rights of others," shall be correctly understood and applied. When examining and determining whether a disputed trademark infringes upon the existing prior rights of others, the people's court shall, for prior rights for which the Trademark Law has special provisions, protect them in accordance with the special provisions of the Trademark Law; for legitimate rights and interests that, although not specifically provided for in the Trademark Law, are entitled to protection under the General Principles of the Civil Law and other laws, protection shall be granted in accordance with this general provision.

The people's court generally takes the filing date of the disputed trademark as the benchmark when examining and determining whether a disputed trademark infringes upon the existing prior rights of others. If the prior right no longer exists at the time of approval for registration of the disputed trademark, it does not affect the registration of the disputed trademark.

18. According to the Trademark Law, an applicant shall not, by unfair means, preemptively register a trademark that has been used by another and has acquired a certain degree of influence. If the applicant knew or should have known that the trademark had been used by another and had acquired a certain degree of influence, and still preemptively registered it, it may be determined that the applicant adopted unfair means.

A trademark that has been actually used within China and is known to a certain range of the relevant public shall be determined as a trademark that has been used and has acquired a certain degree of influence. If there is evidence proving that the prior trademark has been continuously used for a certain period of time, within a certain region, with a certain sales volume, or with a certain amount of advertising or promotion, it may be determined to have a certain degree of influence.

For a trademark that has been used and has acquired a certain degree of influence, it is inappropriate to grant protection on dissimilar goods.

19. When trying administrative cases involving the cancellation of registered trademarks, the people's court shall, in examining and determining whether a disputed trademark was obtained by registration through other unfair means, consider whether it constitutes means other than deceptive means that disrupt the trademark registration order, harm public interests, improperly occupy public resources, or seek illegitimate interests by other means. For circumstances that only damage specific civil rights and interests, the examination and determination shall be conducted in accordance with Article 41, Paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Trademark Law and other corresponding provisions of the Trademark Law.

20. When trying administrative cases involving the cancellation of a registered trademark for non-use for three consecutive years, the people's court shall, in accordance with the legislative intent of the relevant provisions of the Trademark Law, correctly determine whether the act in question constitutes actual use.

The trademark owner's own use, use by licensees with permission, and other uses that do not go against the will of the trademark owner may all be determined as acts of actual use. Even if there are minor differences between the trademark actually used and the trademark approved for registration, if the distinctive features are not altered, it may be regarded as use of the registered trademark. If there is no actual use of the registered trademark, and there are only acts of assignment or licensing, or only publication of trademark registration information or a declaration of exclusive right to the registered trademark, it is inappropriate to determine such acts as trademark use.

If the trademark owner fails to actually use the registered trademark or ceases use due to force majeure, policy restrictions, bankruptcy liquidation, or other objective reasons, or if the trademark owner has a genuine intention to use the trademark and has made necessary preparations for actual use but has not yet actually used the registered trademark due to other objective reasons, it may all be determined that there is a legitimate reason.
